speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The provisions of these two Bills are to implement the changes to our tax regime announced earlier this year in Budget 2024, as well as those arising from other policy reviews.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They are intended to anchor and encourage high-quality investments in Singapore, to grow our economy and create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They are also intended to ensure that our tax system remains relevant and fair to businesses and individuals and align Singapore's tax regime with international tax developments arising from the Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) 2.0 initiative.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Overall, the changes will sustain Singapore's economic competitiveness, provide better support to businesses and individuals, and ensure that Singapore keeps in step with international tax developments.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Ministry of Finance (MOF) sought views from the public on the two draft Bills in June.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We thank the respondents for their feedback and have taken onboard some of the suggestions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The global economic landscape is becoming increasingly competitive, and Singapore needs to keep pace with the competition in order to continue attracting investments to grow our economy and create good jobs for our people.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Other countries around the world are not standing still.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Their governments are rolling out initiatives to attract investments, especially in strategic sectors such as semiconductors and advanced manufacturing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For instance, the United States (US) CHIPS and Science Act sets aside US$53 billion, or about S$70 billion, to support semiconductor manufacturing, research and development (R&D) and workforce development in the US.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In July last year, Germany announced plans to invest around 20 billion euros, or around S$29 billion, as part of the European Union (EU) Chips Act to bolster its semiconductor manufacturing sector.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Japan also announced in November last year that it would allocate two trillion yen, or about S$18 billion to support its semiconductor industry.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Though we cannot match the financial resources of these large economies, we must continue to do our best to remain attractive to investments and encourage business growth in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The RIC will give us a useful tool to attract and support businesses that undertake substantive and high-value economic activities here.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It will allow us to anchor and encourage high-quality investments, create good jobs for Singaporeans and support our green transition.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, let me explain how the RIC will work.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is an expenditure-based grant delivered through the tax system.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These include the development or expansion of manufacturing facilities, setting up of headquarters and services, pursuit of R&D and innovation activities, commodity trading and decarbonisation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These activities and expenditure categories are aligned with the four pillars of our Singapore Economy 2030 vision – trade, enterprise, manufacturing and services – as well as to support our green transition.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The tax credits will be offset against corporate income tax payable in the first instance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If the RIC quantum exceeds the amount of taxes paid by the company, the unutilised credits will be refunded to the company within four years from the time the company makes the claim application in respect of the qualifying expenditures incurred.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This feature is particularly useful for companies in an early stage of growth, where they have yet to turn a profit.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The RIC support will be commensurate with the size and quality of businesses' economic contributions to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will be based on our economic agencies' assessment of how much the projects will bring in, in terms of new fixed asset investment, productive capacity and skilled jobs created for locals, as well as whether the investment involves state-of-the-art technological development, strengthens our competitiveness, builds resilience in our economy and creates broader economic spillovers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Another key amendment in the Bill is on the Renovation and Refurbishment, or R&R scheme for short.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Under our normal tax rules, R&R expenses are not tax-deductible because they are capital in nature.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This is to support small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in customer-facing sectors, like food and beverage (F&B) and retail, which typically need to incur such expenses to enhance their customer service and experience.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We are enhancing the R&R scheme in three ways.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Next, we will standardise the three-year period for determining the expenditure cap for all businesses, instead of having it commence when each business makes its first claim.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Bill will fix the relevant three-year period, with the first three-year period being from YA2025 to YA2027.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will simplify the process and reduce compliance costs for companies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The third enhancement provides all businesses with a permanent option to claim R&R deductions in one YA, instead of over three YAs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This will give businesses more flexibility to manage their cashflow needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These were also announced at this year's Budget.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The two taxes are: first, the domestic top-up tax (DTT); and second, the multinational enterprise top-up tax (MTT).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The MTT applies the Income Inclusion Rule, which is part of the BEPS Pillar Two Global Anti-Base Erosion, or GLoBE rules for short.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MTT will apply to large MNE groups that are parented in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If the effective tax rate of the MNE group's entities in any foreign jurisdiction is below 15%, MTT will be imposed to top up the effective tax rate to 15%.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The implementation of the DTT and MTT ensures that Singapore is aligned with the international implementation of BEPS 2.0.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The EU, the United Kingdom (UK), Switzerland, Japan, Korea, Malaysia and Hong Kong, among other jurisdictions, have either implemented similar rules or intend to do so in 2025.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If we do not impose the DTT and MTT, affected MNE groups would have to pay these taxes to other jurisdictions that have imposed the GLoBE rules.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Hence, it is in Singapore's interest to impose the DTT and MTT, so that we can collect the tax, rather than cede it to other jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the new environment where companies are subjected to a minimum level of tax wherever they operate, ecosystem factors will become increasingly important for companies' business decisions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We plan to reinvest the additional revenues from DTT and MTT to enhance our overall business environment in areas, such as upskilling our workforce, growing a vibrant innovation ecosystem, and providing quality infrastructure and connectivity.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Offences in the Bill include the failure to keep proper records, tax evasion and the obstruction of the Comptroller.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These powers and offences mirror those that already exist under the Income Tax Act and ensure that the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS) has the necessary powers to enforce compliance with the DTT and MTT.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is an important piece of legislation with wide-ranging implications for Singapore's economy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As someone who works in a global investment firm, I am deeply interested in how this Bill will impact both our local and international business environments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While I fully support the principle of global tax fairness as stated in the Bill, I have clarifications about the potential impact on our local businesses and Singapore’s competitive edge in the global market.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Although the Bill primarily targets MNEs, the effects could trickle down.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If MNEs choose to relocate or scale back operations in Singapore, it could hurt SMEs that rely on these larger corporations for business.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Section 14 outlines the top-up tax chargeable on MNEs, but it is critical to consider the ripple effects that this might have on SMEs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These smaller businesses may lose significant revenue if MNEs move to more tax-friendly jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are our local SMEs prepared to adapt if MNEs downsize or leave?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What strategies are in place to help SMEs diversify their business models?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Do we have initiatives to enhance their competitiveness so that they can remain resilient in this shifting landscape?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Government-SME partnerships and incentives for innovation within local industries will be key to help these businesses thrive.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I would also urge that we build in support measures for SMEs to mitigate any negative effects from potential MNE relocations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Sections 31 to 36 deal with registration and record-keeping requirements.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These could be challenging for smaller entities with fewer resources.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Has the Government assessed the compliance costs for these smaller subsidiaries?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Should we consider exemptions or reduced obligations for those that may struggle with these requirements?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, section 36, which imposes surcharges for failure to register, could disproportionately affect these smaller entities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If not handled carefully, these compliance demands could lead to layoffs or reductions in employee benefits.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is important that we consider exemptions or reduced compliance burdens for smaller subsidiaries, to avoid placing unnecessary strain on local businesses and their employees.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, while the MTT is intended to generate additional revenue, there appears to be a lack of clarity on how this revenue will directly benefit Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Section 58 touches on the recovery of unpaid MTT.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, it does not specify how these funds will be allocated for the public good.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This would not only boost public confidence in the Bill, but also ensure transparency and accountability in how the revenue is spent.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These measures will help Singapore remain a competitive and attractive destination for investments while also benefiting our local workforce.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Section 17, which defines the effective tax rate for MNEs, could make Singapore less attractive to foreign investors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If MNEs find more tax-friendly environments elsewhere, we could see companies relocating their operations.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Presently, there have been MNEs moving their headquarters or downsizing their operations in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This could be due to a variety of factors, including costs of business.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This tax regime could further diminish the allure of having a presence in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What measures are in place to prevent this?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This would position Singapore as not only a tax-efficient jurisdiction, but also an innovation-driven economy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, we must not overlook Pillar One of BEPS 2.0, which reallocates taxing rights to the markets where consumers are based.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have proposed several measures in my speech.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, provide targeted relief and resources to help SMEs adapt if MNEs downsize or relocate.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, consider exemptions or reduced compliance requirements for smaller subsidiaries to avoid excessive strain on local businesses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, introduce incentives for supporting initiatives, such as the RIC, and address the implications of Pillar One of BEPS 2.0 to maintain Singapore’s competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Most importantly, we must guarantee that the benefits of this new tax regime are tangible within our own communities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Corporations that have thrived in Singapore on our good governance, infrastructure and talent pool should contribute to the public good.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must use the additional tax revenue to strengthen our public infrastructure, enhance healthcare services and upskill our workforce, ensuring that Singaporeans see and feel the direct benefits.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure that our policies support economic resilience and social equity while keeping Singapore an attractive hub for global businesses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This will allow others to capture tax revenue that we otherwise could.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Given our well-telegraphed future expenditure needs, this would be foolhardy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For these reasons, the Workers’ Party supports the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even so, some may caution that subscribing to a corporate minimum tax will erode some of the cornerstones of Singapore’s global competitiveness: our attractiveness to foreign capital.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In my speech, I will explain why such fears are probably misplaced and what we can do to avoid it.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Absent low taxes, they say, we will be unable to attract the necessary investments from abroad which, in turn, will leave us adrift.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If there were any truth to such a claim, it would perhaps have been applicable half a century ago.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is no secret that, in Singapore, in our formative years as a nation, we did, indeed, rely heavily on attracting foreign direct investments via multinationals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This, in turn, hinged on factors, such as attractive corporate incentives, including tax holidays for multinationals, which kept the effective company tax rate as low as 10%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, even a casual examination of statutory corporate tax rates would reveal that statutory rates were as high as 40% until the late 1980s.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It was only later that they were progressively reduced to 32% through the early 1990s, then 26%, then to the 17% that prevails today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Whether this was a belated effort to chase the tail of low costs to sustain our competitive edge, or if it was driven by pressure from foreign businesses to keep rates attractive, I do not know.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What I do know is my belief that we should already have evolved away from such unvarnished tax competition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The determinants of foreign direct investments are, after all, rich and varied.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But there is only some mild indication that the corporate tax rate, whether statutory or effective, matters.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, one study that summarised the extant evidence suggests that factors like market size, trade openness and infrastructure quality are between four and seven times more important.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another concluded that: “the effect that tax policy had on foreign direct investment (FDI) was small compared to other factors” and that “tax policy cannot compensate for a negative investment climate”.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One important reason for this relatively muted effect of taxes on FDI is that sufficiently large MNCs will, ultimately, confront foreign taxes on their earnings when their profits are repatriated back to their home country anyway.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This could even lead, paradoxically, to a situation where, depending on the tax regime of the home country, raising taxes may even stimulate more investment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, tax treaties designed to mitigate the effects of double taxation may blunt this effect somewhat.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, such treaties have often been found to have little effect on actual FDI flows.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such conditions are precisely what are being addressed by BEPS 2.0.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The new regime targets large MNCs, many of which are already domiciled in higher-tax regimes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While these home countries can now officially apply a top-up tax, many firms would have faced such higher taxes anyway when profits were eventually booked at home for redistribution to shareholders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, my sense is that while BEPS 2.0 may hurt at the margin, it is far from being game-changing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a high-income economy, Singapore’s attractiveness as an investment destination is not, and should not, be fundamentally reliant on low corporate taxes, but on all the other things that set us apart.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Lest one takes this as an idiosyncratic opinion, I should stress that this is not just my own conclusion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, our score on the Global Competitiveness Report is due more to our country's transport and utility infrastructure, sophisticated and stable financial system and quality of institutions, as opposed to low taxes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The reality is that our competitiveness is not anchored in low taxes and it is also reflected in real world investment advisory.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: PwC, the corporate advisory lists – in a 2022 report – 10 factors that make Singapore the best in class in the region and none of these 10 are about taxes, per se.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To the extent that taxes were featured at all, it was in the context of double taxation agreements, which I agree should continue to be a priority for IRAS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is not to say that foreign investment is not important.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Rather, it is that we should pursue FDI more for its secondary benefits, rather than for the financing itself.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Where we have fallen short, rather, has been in bringing our levels of productivity and innovative capacity to the global frontier.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What should, instead, become ever-more important is a focus on elevating the efficiency of our capital deployment and an upgrading of our technological capabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If we are not to expend our efforts in courting global capital, then, what should we do instead?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We should reinvest as much as possible in the human capital of our people, of course, as this will bring not only more bang for the buck, it also comes with improved productivity and innovation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Notwithstanding how money is ultimately fungible, this implies that we should, nevertheless, seriously consider earmarking the funds for R&D, education, or, as my Sengkang colleague will suggest later in his speech, healthcare.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In prior interventions in this House, I had repeatedly emphasised the importance of placing the investment in human capital on at least the same footing as that of physical capital.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I had suggested, for example, that funds targeted toward infrastructure development can and should be broadened to accommodate expenditure on training and education or warned that those deigned for productivity improvements do not somehow get diverted toward yet more physical capital accumulation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At risk of oversimplification, Mr Speaker, let me offer an analogy to the points I am making.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We can think of tax rates as parking fees one pays to access a mall.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Sure, all else equal, one would probably choose a mall that charges less for parking or offers free parking for the first hour or two.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But ultimately, we choose the mall we do because of the range of shops, the price of the goods that are sold there, the quality and service of its restaurants and how pleasant the overall shopping experience is.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such thrusts should be the focus of our investment regime, going forward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In future, we are likely to see more, not less, of such multilateral economic agreements, led by the major economies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Similar progress has been made, within the G20, on the rollout of a global wealth tax.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The reality is, international agreements that used to sting as a result of difficulties associated with free-riding, are now finding renewed life, via unilateral mechanisms by major players that better align the incentives of those that would previously have rankled at the prospect of such coordination.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It behooves us to play to our nation's inherent advantages, as they exist today and not as they used to be, as we navigate this changing global geoeconomic and political landscape.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I support the Bill but I have some clarifications to seek from the Minister.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The rules under the MMT Bill implement Pillar Two of the OECD/G20 BEPS framework.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This move reflects our commitment to ensuring fair taxation while continuing to position Singapore as an attractive destination for business and investment.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My first clarification has to do with how these new rules fit in with our existing tax treaty network.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: According to IRAS, Singapore has signed a number of Avoidance of Double Taxation Agreements (DTAs) and these include limited DTAs and Exchange of Information Arrangements.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: At the moment, we have concluded treaties with around 100 jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These treaties have set a firm foundation for us to do business with countries all over the world and they provide certainty on cross-border tax positions.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The new Pillar Two rules deviate from the traditional source and residence-based rules of taxation which our existing tax treaty network is built on and they introduce an additional layer of taxation on profits that may have already been allocated and taxed under treaties.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Will more detailed guidance be issued on how Pillar Two rules will affect the application of Singapore's current network of DTAs, if at all?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Presently, the United States (US) and China which are the two major economies in the world, as well as key trading partners of Singapore, these two countries have not yet adopted these rules.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Does MOF have clarity on how Singapore might be affected if we enact the MMT Bill, but the US and China do not go ahead to implement Pillar Two?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, I note that Pillar Two rules are generally enacted through domestic legislation in each participating country.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Despite the OECD's Model Rules serving as a foundation, variations will inevitably arise between jurisdictions, in how the rules are written, interpreted and enforced.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These differences could lead to prolonged disputes due to unintended consequences or inconsistent application of the Pillar Two rules across different jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: MOF has replied in its response to the public consultation on this Bill that the dispute resolution process for Pillar Two matters is presently under discussion by the Inclusive Framework for the global implementation of the BEPS Project.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Would the Minister be able to provide a timeframe as to when we can expect to see guidance being issued on these processes?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong commented in this year's Budget Statement that the implementation of BEPS Pillar Two initiatives will provide additional revenues to the Government in the short term.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: However, he noted that it was "uncertain" as to how much this additional revenue would amount to, or for how long it would last.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: He stated that Singapore may even see a reduction in its tax base, should MNEs choose to shift some of their activities to other jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If so, has the Government considered how to mitigate any employment or other losses that might result from MNEs leaving Singapore?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Although Pillar Two targets large MNEs, its influence will also extend to other areas of Singapore's business landscape.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Smaller firms connected to these MNEs, such as suppliers and service providers, could feel the indirect impact.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is a point that the hon Member Mr Yip Hon Weng has brought up as well.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, if a major company adjusts its operations to better align with new tax requirements, for example, if it shifts its production to a different country or it alters its procurement strategies, this could significantly disrupt its current relationships with local businesses.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Its local suppliers may face reduced demand for their products and service partners could see decreased revenue as well.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: What is the Government's outlook on these broader effects and are there any specific challenges that the Government can see at this point in time, which are coming for non-MNEs, with the introduction of the new Pillar Two rules?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To say that the new Pillar Two rules are Byzantine would really be a severe understatement.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: They import OECD principles and guidelines into our domestic legislation and these are extremely complicated rules.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: We are not alone in facing this challenge.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Many other countries that have implemented Pillar Two rules also faced similar problems with implementation.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In many ways, Pillar Two represents a fundamental shift in the way that we view international tax rules.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My next clarifications pertain to how ready businesses are to implement these rules.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Compliance with Pillar Two rules will impose additional reporting requirements and prohibitive costs on MNEs.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: They will need to navigate much more complex tax regulations.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To this end, I would like to ask if the Government has any plans to assist to MNEs to meet their new enhanced compliance obligations.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, where there are new and complicated rules to apply, there will also be plenty of opportunities.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Trained tax professionals should be able to rise to the challenge of the expanded demand for well-qualified service providers.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: On this point, will the Government be committing any resources towards the training or re-training of local tax professionals so that they may be well-equipped to serve the demands of this changing tax environment.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Here, I declare my interest as a part-time lecturer in international tax and trade at the Nanyang Technological University.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In my personal role as an educator, I see many young people with a keen interest in international tax developments.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My own class enrolment has quadrupled over the space of around five years.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As we move into a world defined by the developing rules of the BEPs project, would the Government consider devoting more resources to the development of international tax education in Singapore at the tertiary level and beyond?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Rather, in order to encourage and retain foreign investment, countries will need to present other attractive factors, such as a skilled workforce, political stability, excellent infrastructure, a strong legal system and perhaps, more importantly, a high quality of life.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To the specific point of being able to offer our residents a good quality of life, let us not forget that a thriving arts and cultural scene is one of the linchpins of a vibrant and dynamic society.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As noted by a 2021 report from United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization and the World Bank, culture and creativity contribute to a so-called "amenity effect" and this is where people and businesses prefer to dwell in places that "foster social interaction and knowledge spillovers".

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The report also refers to the work of urban economist Richard Florida, who has developed a gauge referred to as the "Bohemian Index".

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: With it, he measures the numbers of certain types of creatives, such as writers, actors and musicians, who are located in different regions and cities.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is a sector that is not only tied specifically to our creative economy, but to the general well-being of society and the attractiveness of Singapore as a whole.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: A thriving arts and cultural scene is the lifeblood of a vibrant city.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It draws talent, inspires creativity and will make us a magnet for global talent and businesses.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This will mark a major shift in Singapore's taxation policy, which the Progressive Singapore Party (PSP) supports.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP believes that more profitable companies should pay more taxes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I first articulated this policy position during my Budget speech in 2023.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During that speech, I also spoke about the highly inequitable nature of our corporate tax system, where companies with the highest profits pay the lowest percentage of their profits as tax.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, I pointed out that companies earning profits before tax of between $200,000 and $10 million paid on average 8% to 9% of their profits as taxes, whereas companies with profits beyond $1 billion pay less than 1% of their profits as taxes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We hope that the introduction of a minimum effective tax rate for MNEs under this Bill will make for a more equitable corporate taxation system where large MNEs pay their fair share of taxes relative to their profits.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have debated the impact of this Bill on tax revenue before in this House and it is likely to be substantial, especially considering recent data showing strong corporate earnings following the post-COVID-19 economic recovery.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The OECD's 2024 Corporate Tax Statistics report showed that large MNEs accounted for 73% of total corporate income tax revenue in 2021.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If investments and business activities in Singapore remain the same, then we are likely to soon see a very substantial increase in corporate tax revenues.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During the Budget debate in 2022, the Finance Minister cautioned that "BEPS 2.0 represents a fundamental change in the competitive environment for Singapore" and we would likely "need to find other ways to stay competitive, from investing even more in our workers to building new infrastructure and incentivising R&D", and any additional tax revenue from Pillars One and Two would need to be reinvested to ensure Singapore remains competitive.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2023, he again said that "we cannot afford to price ourselves out of the competition, or else Singapore and Singaporeans will end up the biggest losers".

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singapore does have inherent disadvantages, such as limited land, a small population and a high-cost structure.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we also have strong advantages compared to other countries in the region, such as a highly educated workforce, a well-developed and globally-connected financial system, excellent international connectivity for the movement of people and cargo, respect for rule of law and strong property rights.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These advantages will not go away, even after the provisions of the Bill come into effect.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is highly unlikely that all the MNEs in Singapore will pack up and leave overnight just because there will be a minimum effective tax rate after this Bill is passed.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What this Bill does represent is a once-in-a-generation opportunity to reshape our tax and incentive structure for companies and our policy towards attracting foreign investments.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For many decades, we have used various tax incentives and schemes to lower effective corporate tax rates and attract foreign investments, especially from MNEs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But such a strategy could never have lasted forever.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Other countries could and did replicate Singapore's tax incentives, in whole or in part, creating a destructive race to the bottom where governments across the world slashed corporate tax rates to attract businesses.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This trend has only stabilised in recent years with BEPS 2.0.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This imposition of a global minimum corporate tax regime is a step in the right direction that has hastened the inevitable for our nation, which is, the need to make ourselves competitive and attractive to foreign investments in ways other than providing them with economic incentives and low taxes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As I mentioned earlier, we still have strong advantages as a nation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the additional economic resources that this Bill provides will allow us to do more.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the additional tax revenue from this Bill, we can help to create a more level playing field between domestic companies and MNEs.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many of the MNEs in Singapore are foreign-owned, and this dependency has increased in recent years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And finally, we can take steps to address our high cost structure.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In particular, PSP feels that the rising rent and cost of property is an area that requires urgent attention.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, the Multinational Enterprise (Minimum Tax) Bill we are debating today marks a significant change in Singapore's tax policy.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We believe that more profitable companies should pay more taxes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As I have pointed out in my 2023 Budget speech, our current corporate tax system is highly inequitable, with the most profitable companies paying the lowest percentage of their profits in income tax.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For a long time, our country has relied on low tax rates and tax incentives to attract foreign investments.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: After this Bill is passed, we will no longer be able to rely on these measures to attract foreign investment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Bill provides our country with a rare opportunity to transform our corporate tax and incentive structure as well as our policies for attracting foreign investment.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our corporate tax revenue currently heavily depends on foreign multinational enterprises.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must also create a fairer competition environment between local companies and multinational corporations.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In particular, the rise in property prices and rents needs urgent attention.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP sincerely hopes that our fourth-generation leaders will use this opportunity to reshape our economic structure, renew our social contract and create a better living environment for Singaporeans. : This Bill presents us with an opportunity to reshape our economic structure and refresh our social compact, instead of using it towards the same economic playbook that has been used for decades.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP hopes that the 4G leadership will make full use of this opportunity.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is a topic which I feel strongly about and have spoken on many occasions, including the last four Budget debates from 2021 to 2024.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As Singapore is one of the 147 countries who are members of the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework, it is important that at the heart of it all, we adhere to the principles of BEPS and why a global tax consensus on this matter is so important.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The rules are designed to ensure that large MNEs pay a minimum level of tax on their income in each jurisdiction where they operate, thereby reducing the incentive for profit shifting and placing a floor under tax competition and bringing an end to the race to the bottom on corporate tax rates.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This can only be beneficial to all countries, including Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In Singapore, corporate income tax is by far the single largest contributor to the Government's budget, more so than the Net Investment Returns Contribution, personal income taxes or even the Goods and Services Tax (GST).

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Any changes to our corporate income tax policies are going to have the most significant impact to our country's operating revenues, and by extension, our long-term fiscal position and fiscal strategies; that is, if we allow it to be as such, as I will be elaborating further in my speech.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Beyond the technicalities of the tax legislation to be implemented, my first question is on MOF's assessment of the scope and impact of this new legislation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Just how many of such MNE groups are operating in Singapore as of today, what is their total reported revenues, profits before taxes, corporate income taxes paid to Singapore and their effective tax rates?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, as with the past decades, many MNEs operating here in Singapore are given various tax incentive schemes and these include the pioneer industries and service companies' incentive, development and expansion incentive, investment allowances, concessionary tax rates for global trading companies, finance and treasury centres, maritime sector incentives – just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How many of these incentive schemes will still be in force by the time this Bill is operationalised, and what would happen to the effective tax rates of the companies who are currently enjoying these preferential schemes?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Would the top-up taxes prescribed by Pillar Two supersede these schemes?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am reminded of an article on Bloomberg in 2021, which looked into the data collected by the US Internal Revenue Service on US companies' country-by-country filings on where they book their profits and pay taxes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is quite clear to everyone that our statutory corporate income tax rate of 17% in Singapore is low by global standards.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But especially with the whole suite of tax incentives on offer, our effective corporate income tax rates are even lower, with some companies under the pioneer tax incentive scheme effectively paying no taxes for a number of years; and companies under various other schemes effectively having tax rates as low as 5%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Mathematically speaking, it is thus not hard to imagine the potential increase in corporate income tax revenues from implementing a minimum tax rate of 15%, especially when many of these tax-incentivised companies are likely to be the ones who fall under the scope of the Pillar Two rules.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What then is the Government's assessment of the potential increase in tax revenues when changes in this Act are implemented from 2025?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In my Budget 2024 debate speech, I shared that the OECD has published a working paper earlier this year, which finds that the global minimum tax "can raise between US$155 billion and US$192 billion of additional CIT revenues per year, with revenue gains accruing to all jurisdiction groups".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, estimated participating countries categorised as "investment hubs", which includes Singapore, would have the largest expected gains from the reforms, with corporate income tax revenues rising from 14% minimum to up to 34%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Will the Minister now be able to provide an update given that most other countries would have enacted or are in the process of enacting these legislations and MNEs would have to adhere to the same set of rules internationally from 2025?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My second question, is the Government's plan to effectively return any additional corporate income tax revenues back to these in-scope MNEs, such that we will not have any additional net revenues going forward?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In Budget 2024, RIC was introduced, which is to be awarded on qualifying expenditures incurred by a company in respect of a qualifying project, during the qualifying period.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: According to IRAS' website, the credits are to be offset against Corporate Income Tax payable.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is introduced in the new section 93B under the Income Tax (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Qualifying expenditure, for example, covers a whole range of categories including capital expenditure, manpower costs, training costs, professional fees, intangible asset costs, fees for work outsourced in Singapore, materials and consumables and freight and logistics costs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Are there expenditures that do not actually qualify and how would EDB or EnterpriseSG make such a determination as to what activities and expenditure would qualify under RIC and whether objective criteria on the assessment of the quantum of RIC to be awarded will be published in due course?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In my view, the effectiveness of the MNE Bill and the amount of net revenues we collect from in-scope MNEs will substantially depend on the extent of the generosity of EDB and EnterpriseSG towards these MNEs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What I am also concerned about is that under subsection 51 of the Income Tax (Amendment) Bill, "The Minister may make regulations to carry out the purposes and provisions of this section".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This gives the Minister a broad mandate to make regulations concerning RICs and there are two particular areas which I hope the Minister can provide further clarifications on.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What is the rationale for this, how will this be applied and will the Government end up incurring out-of-pocket expenditure, as though it is a grant being given to the company?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Second, under subsection 46, the company can apply for RICs to be given to offset any taxes of one or more of its other related companies under the same group.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Would this not go against the principle that RIC is granted to incentivise certain specific economic activities by certain entities and for certain qualifying expenditure only?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Again, what is the rationale for this and how will this be applied?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My third question, which is arguably a rhetorical one, is does the Government see Singapore as just another a tax haven?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For avoidance of doubt, I strongly believe that we are not a tax haven.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A few weeks ago, Singapore was ranked second in the IMD's World Talent Ranking and fourth in the world financial centres ranking.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In June this year, Singapore took the top spot in the IMD World Competitiveness Ranking and, in January, Singapore was ranked the most liveable city for Asian expatriates, among others.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To quote an International Tax and Transaction Services Leader in one of the Big Four Accounting firms, "overall, for the smaller nations like Singapore, the curtailing of tax competition from the global minimum tax proposal will drive a greater focus on economic fundamentals.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Singapore's long-standing merits in its institutions, infrastructure, labor market and financial and legal systems – qualities it has conscientiously nurtured for decades – would arguably be an even greater source of distinctiveness." Should the rollout of the global minimum tax be proceeding as scheduled, I would say, yes, let us not be complacent, but we should take this window of opportunity to adapt and innovate when it comes to considering new economic development models that are more sustainable and less reliant on short-term tax incentives.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Let us also be a bit prouder of our non-tax advantages, including our most important asset, Singaporeans themselves, and not fall prey to the thinking that without aggressive tax incentives, we would not be competitive to international MNEs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Lastly, in addition to GloBE rules, Pillar Two also includes a Subject-to-Tax Rule (STTR).

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: STTR allows a developing country to impose additional taxes of up to 9% on certain payments, such as interest and royalties, that an entity makes to related entities in another jurisdiction, if that payment is taxed at less than 9% in the other jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In September last month, I note that nine jurisdictions signed a new multilateral treaty that will allow early adopters to swiftly implement the new Pillar Two STTR, with 57 countries attending the first signing ceremony of the Multilateral Convention.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The OECD has stated that the STTR is an integral part of the consensus achieved on Pillar Two and is especially important for developing Inclusive Framework members.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As the Government often reiterates that Singapore is a developing country, can I confirm with the Minister that Singapore is considered a developing country under STTR and will be able to benefit from this rule?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Allow me to conclude, Mr Speaker, by returning to the first principles of BEPS 2.0, which is that these reforms were introduced to stop the race to the bottom when it comes to sovereign tax policies and to facilitate international collaboration to end tax avoidance.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And by supporting BEPS 2.0, we not only promote a more equitable tax system but also signal our commitment to responsible global governance and economic fairness, thereby dissociating ourselves from the terms tax havens or tax-favoured jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is perfectly reasonable for the Government to reinvest additional tax revenues, such as through this landmark global tax reform into Singapore's developmental needs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   The MTT provisions, from clauses 21 to 36, are aligned with the global consensus to combat tax avoidance strategies among large MNEs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Are there robust mechanisms in place to ensure consistency across jurisdictions, avoiding discrepancies in tax treatment?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore has built its success as a global hub for MNEs by maintaining an attractive tax environment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While the introduction of this global minimum tax is important, we must not lose sight of the competitive edge that has made Singapore a top choice for businesses.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I urge the Government to consider complementary measures, such as enhancing R&D incentives and talent acquisition programmes, to continue attracting investment in key sectors.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These additional policies can ensure that we remain competitive, despite the increasing global tax harmonisation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, if fewer MNCs come to Singapore, it will not benefit our SME ecosystem, and fewer good jobs will be created.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Maintaining our appeal to MNEs is essential for supporting both the broader business landscape and job creation. : Clauses 37 to 94 introduce new registration and compliance requirements.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I urge the Government to carefully assess the administrative burden this will place on both the Government and MNEs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will the Comptroller's office be adequately resourced to manage this increased workload?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, what measures are in place to assist businesses in navigating these complex compliance frameworks, especially in the early stages of the implementation?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Clear guidance and streamlined processes will be crucial to ensure smooth compliance and avoid stifling business operations through excessive bureaucracy.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One specific area of concern is the treatment of joint ventures and investment entities.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Could this exclusion incentivise certain entities to exploit the system and avoid paying their fair share of the top-up taxes?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I seek clarification on how the Government plans to ensure that these exclusions do not inadvertently open doors to aggressive tax planning.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Bill's provisions under clauses 49 to 55 allow for a 15-month filing period after the financial year-end, which aligns with the international norms.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, given the complexities of multi-jurisdictional operations, I ask: could we consider offering grace periods or additional guidance for entities facing exceptional circumstances?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, the penalties for late payments and non-compliance should deter misconduct without overburdening businesses facing administrative challenges.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I propose that we channel these funds into strategic areas that will directly benefit Singaporeans, such as sustainability initiatives, green infrastructure projects and education programmes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By investing in these areas, we can further strengthen our long-term economic goals while enhancing Singapore's competitiveness in the global arena.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, as we implement these changes, we must safeguard our competitive advantage and ensure that businesses are not unduly burdened by compliance requirements.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I look forward to the Minister's response and trust that we can continue to strike a careful balance between global alignment and protecting Singapore's economic interests.
